content: Hypoglycemia is a pathological condition characterized by abnormally low levels of glucose in the blood. It typically occurs when blood glucose levels fall below 60 to 70 mg/dL, although different thresholds (e.g., below 40, 50, 60, or 70 mg/dL) are used to define low glucose levels. Patients with type 1 diabetes may experience an average of two symptomatic hypoglycemic episodes per week, accumulating thousands of such episodes over their lifetime, with at least one severe episode annually. The causes of hypoglycemia vary by age. In neonates, causes include transient neonatal hypoglycemia, prematurity, intrauterine growth retardation, perinatal asphyxia, sepsis, congenital hypopituitarism, congenital hyperinsulinism, infants of diabetic mothers, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism. In adults, hypoglycemia is primarily caused by insulin or insulin secretagogue drugs, alcohol, hepatic failure, renal failure, cardiac failure, sepsis, non-islet cell pancreatic tumors, insulinoma, and reactive hypoglycemia. The pathophysiology of hypoglycemia involves the failure of physiological defense mechanisms and hormones, such as insulin, glucagon, and epinephrine, to restore normal glucose levels. These defense mechanisms primarily regulate glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. No single glucose value alone defines hypoglycemia; instead, diagnostic criteria, such as Whipple's triad, are used. This triad includes symptoms of hypoglycemia, low plasma glucose levels correlated with symptoms, and symptom resolution upon glucose correction. Complications of hypoglycemia in adults include an increased risk of dementia, cardiovascular complications, and potentially death. The prognosis is generally favorable with prompt treatment, but 4–10% of deaths in patients with type 1 diabetes are attributed to hypoglycemia. Screening for hypoglycemia is essential in at-risk infants, with surveillance recommended every three to six hours during the first 48 hours of life. Treatment should begin immediately after initial blood tests without waiting for confirmatory laboratory results due to the high risk of neurological damage. Medical treatment for hypoglycemia depends on the severity of symptoms and the underlying cause. For asymptomatic cases, repeating glucose measurements and avoiding critical tasks may suffice. In symptomatic or severe cases, 20 grams of glucose is typically sufficient to raise blood glucose levels. Glucose can be administered subcutaneously, intramuscularly, or intravenously as 25% dextrose serum. For postprandial hypoglycemia, patients should consume frequent small meals or snacks high in fiber while avoiding high-sugar foods. Surgery is the preferred treatment for insulinoma. Hypoglycemia was first identified in 1922 by James Collip during his work on purifying insulin. He observed a reduction in blood glucose levels after injecting insulin into a rabbit, which led to coma and death when a large dose was administered. Hypoglycemia can be classified by severity into five categories: severe hypoglycemia, symptomatic hypoglycemia, asymptomatic hypoglycemia, probable symptomatic hypoglycemia, and pseudo-hypoglycemia. It can also be categorized as mild, moderate, or severe. The pathophysiology of hypoglycemia involves the failure of counterregulatory hormones, such as insulin, glucagon, and epinephrine, to correct low glucose levels. Insulinomas are rare benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arising from β-islet cells, often associated with mutations in the mTOR/P70S6K signaling pathway. Non-islet cell tumors (NICTH) are large mesenchymal or epithelial tumors that increase glucose utilization and inhibit hepatic glucose release due to the production of incompletely processed IGF-2. On gross pathology, insulinomas appear as small, encapsulated, gray to red-brown tumors, typically solitary. Microscopic findings include trabecular, gyriform, lobular, or solid structures, often with amyloid deposits in a fibrovascular stroma. Immunohistochemical staining for chromogranin A, synaptophysin, and Ki-67 index is used for evaluation. The causes of hypoglycemia in neonates include transient neonatal hypoglycemia, prematurity, intrauterine growth retardation, perinatal asphyxia, sepsis, congenital hypopituitarism, beta-sympathomimetic drugs, congenital hyperinsulinism, infants of diabetic mothers, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and inborn errors of carbohydrate metabolism. In adults, causes include insulin or insulin secretagogue drugs, alcohol, hepatic failure, renal failure, cardiac failure, sepsis, non-islet cell pancreatic tumors, insulinoma, reactive hypoglycemia, post-gastric bypass hypoglycemia, and autoimmune hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemia must be differentiated from other causes of autonomic hyperactivity symptoms. Neonatal hypoglycemia should be distinguished from other causes of neurological symptoms in neonates, such as sepsis, metabolic diseases (e.g., urea cycle disorders, branched-chain organic acidemias), hyponatremia, and neonatal asphyxia. In adults, it should be differentiated from conditions causing autonomic hyperactivity, such as hyperthyroidism, anxiety, arrhythmia, and pheochromocytoma. Patients with type 1 diabetes may experience an average of two symptomatic hypoglycemic episodes per week, with thousands of episodes over their lifetime and one severe episode annually. Hypoglycemia is less common in type 2 diabetes. The event rate for severe hypoglycemia ranges from 40% to 100% in type 1 diabetes. There is no racial or gender predilection for hypoglycemia. Risk factors for hypoglycemia include excessive insulin doses in diabetic patients, especially after missed meals or exercise. Nocturnal fasting and alcohol intake are less common risk factors in diabetic patients. Screening for hypoglycemia is essential in at-risk infants, with surveillance every three to six hours during the first 48 hours of life. Treatment should begin immediately after primary blood tests without waiting for confirmatory laboratory results due to the high risk of neurological damage. If left untreated, hypoglycemia can progress to anxiety, nervousness, tremor, palpitations, and sweating. Common complications include psychomotor retardation, epilepsy, and prematurity in neonates. In adults, complications include an increased risk of dementia, cardiovascular complications, and death. The prognosis is generally good, but 4–10% of deaths in type 1 diabetes are due to hypoglycemia. Diagnostic criteria for hypoglycemia include symptoms of hypoglycemia, low plasma glucose levels correlated with symptoms, and symptom resolution upon glucose correction (Whipple's triad). Neonatal hypoglycemia can be diagnosed by measuring plasma insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate, blood pH, bicarbonate, lactate, free fatty acids, acylcarnitine profile, and plasma free and total carnitine levels. Hypoglycemic symptoms can be divided into those caused by counterregulatory hormones (e.g., anxiety, nervousness, tremor, palpitations, sweating) and neuroglycopenic symptoms (e.g., irritability, weakness, apathy, lethargy, confusion, amnesia). Physical examination findings include tachycardia, ventricular arrhythmia, altered mental status, hypotonia, and motor deficits. Neonatal signs include large-for-gestational-age infants, hepatomegaly in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, and ambiguous genitalia in congenital adrenal insufficiency. Laboratory investigations include plasma glucose (<55–70 mg/dL), insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, sulfonylurea screen, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and 24-hour fasting glucose levels. On EKG, hypoglycemia is characterized by sinus tachycardia and supraventricular tachycardia. Chest X-rays show no findings in hypoglycemia. CT scans can diagnose insulinomas and islet-cell hypertrophy, with insulinomas appearing hypervascular. MRI is more sensitive than CT, showing low intensity on T1-weighted and high intensity on T2-weighted images. Transabdominal ultrasound has low sensitivity for detecting insulinomas. Medical treatment depends on symptom severity and etiology. Asymptomatic cases may require repeated glucose measurements and avoiding critical tasks. Severe cases require 20 grams of glucose, administered subcutaneously, intramuscularly, or intravenously. Postprandial hypoglycemia is managed with frequent small meals high in fiber and low in sugar. Surgery is the treatment of choice for insulinomas. Primary prevention involves patient education on symptoms, blood glucose control, and treatment. Reactive hypoglycemia prevention includes dietary changes, such as smaller meals and avoiding excessive sugar intake. Secondary prevention mirrors primary prevention.
